profiles.meeting_scenario: A university-based interdisciplinary research lab is preparing a brainstorming session for a new review-and-outlook paper on emerging trends in blockchain technology and applications, intended for submission to a high-impact information systems journal. The meeting is between the lead faculty researcher and the lab's research strategy analyst to generate and narrow candidate angles for how the review should go beyond a standard literature summary. The agenda is to brainstorm possible organizing frameworks, decide what kinds of blockchain applications and trend signals should be included, and identify a practical structure for a 'review and outlook' section that can support a publishable contribution. The expected outcome is a short list of 3-4 promising framing ideas and a shared sense of what a usable evidence base and outlook section will look like.

members.name: Dr. Leila Farooq
members.expertise: Blockchain systems, distributed computing, and technical review papers
members.background: Leila leads an interdisciplinary lab that studies emerging digital infrastructure and has previously published technical surveys on consensus protocols, enterprise blockchain architectures, and security issues in decentralized applications.
members.private_state: She wants the paper to look technically authoritative enough to appeal to computing reviewers while still being broad enough to attract citations; she is also quietly trying to avoid a time-consuming full systematic review protocol because the lab has limited bandwidth this semester.
hidden_assumptions: A 'review and outlook' can rely on a strategically curated corpus of the most visible blockchain papers rather than an exhaustive database sweep, as long as the framing is rigorous.

When discussing 'applications,' readers mainly expect implemented or at least architecturally specified blockchain use cases such as supply chains, identity, healthcare, and finance rather than purely conceptual policy discussions.
An 'outlook' section should project near-term technical research directions that emerge from the literature, typically over the next 2-3 years.

If the team says they will cover the 'core blockchain literature,' that naturally includes major computer science conference proceedings and widely cited pre-standardization technical venues, not only journals.
A useful brainstorming outcome is a structure that can be executed quickly with the sources the lab already knows and can access.

members.name: Evan Morales
members.expertise: Bibliometrics, evidence synthesis design, and interdisciplinary trend mapping
members.background: Evan supports faculty across engineering and business schools by designing review methodologies, citation analyses, and publication positioning strategies for cross-domain topics.
members.private_state: He wants the paper to be methodologically defensible to reviewers outside computer science and hopes to shape it into a visibly systematic evidence synthesis that can later be repurposed into a funded research roadmap.
hidden_assumptions: A 'review and outlook' aimed at a high-impact journal should be anchored in a reproducible and explicitly bounded evidence collection process, even if the meeting treats that as background.
When discussing 'applications,' it is natural to include policy pilots, governance models, central bank digital currency initiatives, and adoption frameworks alongside deployed technical systems.
An 'outlook' should identify medium-horizon trajectories in the field, roughly 5-10 years, especially ecosystem and regulatory shifts rather than only immediate technical next steps.

If the team says they will use the 'core blockchain literature,' that usually means indexed journal articles and review papers from stable databases such as Web of Science or Scopus, with conference papers used sparingly.
A productive brainstorming meeting should produce a framework that can survive methodological scrutiny from interdisciplinary reviewers even if some technical breadth is sacrificed.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a 'systematic' review base
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the paper should have a 'systematic backbone' or be 'systematic enough.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a disciplined but selectively curated review of highly influential blockchain work, using known landmark papers, key venues, and targeted database checks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a reproducible evidence-synthesis process with explicit search strings, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and a bounded indexed corpus.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are experienced academics who routinely use the word 'systematic' positively and cooperatively; in a brainstorming meeting, they treat methodology as already broadly understood and do not yet drill into protocol details.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the review should highlight 'applications across domains.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes domains where blockchain systems or prototypes are technically instantiated, such as logistics traceability, decentralized identity, healthcare records, and DeFi platforms.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this also includes governance programs, regulatory sandboxes, CBDC pilots, public-sector adoption frameworks, and organizational experimentation where the blockchain layer may be partial or not fully deployed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'applications across domains' sounds naturally broad and high-level, so each person silently maps it onto their own familiar examples without noticing that their inclusion boundaries differ.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the article needs a strong 'outlook' section.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes a strong outlook is one that identifies technically plausible next-wave research problems and architectures likely to matter in the next 2-3 years.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes a strong outlook is one that maps broader field trajectories and adoption conditions over a 5-10 year horizon, including regulation, standards, and institutional uptake.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In review writing, 'outlook' is a standard, seemingly unproblematic term; both members think they are adding value by strengthening it, but they apply different time horizons and standards for what makes it substantive.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention grounding the brainstorm in the 'core blockchain literature from 2013 onward.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of seminal blockchain papers including major IEEE/ACM conference proceedings, influential technical surveys, and classic architecture/security papers that shaped the field's early discourse.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of indexed journal and review articles retrievable from Web of Science or Scopus, with emphasis on stable bibliometric records from 2013 onward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each person assumes the phrase 'core literature' transparently points to the obvious foundational corpus in their own professional practice, and because both corpora overlap somewhat, the divergence remains hidden during broad planning.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to read as technically serious, not like a generic interdisciplinary scan. If we position it as a review and outlook, we can make it useful for newer researchers without committing ourselves to a full systematic-review apparatus. The outlook, to me, should point to the next couple of years of technical problems the field is actually moving toward.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Evan. I think we have a real opportunity to do a review-and-outlook piece on blockchain trends that feels current, technically credible, and genuinely useful for people entering the area. If we get the balance right, it can be more than a summary and still land with a broad readership.

turns.inner_thought: Good—if we can make this look methodologically defensible from the start, it has a much better chance with a high-impact information systems journal. By systematic backbone, I mean an explicit evidence-synthesis design with a bounded indexed corpus and reproducible retrieval. And the evolution story since 2013 should rest on stable records that outside reviewers will trust.

turns.inner_thought: Starting from the core blockchain literature from 2013 onward gives us a manageable base—major architecture, consensus, security, and enterprise papers, including the key conference work everyone in computing knows. Then we can cluster applications around the domains where systems and prototypes are actually built, not drift into abstract policy terrain.
turns.utterance: One practical way to start is by grounding the brainstorm in the core blockchain literature from 2013 onward and then clustering the material around a few big buckets: consensus, security, enterprise platforms, and applications across domains. That would give us a structure people can recognize immediately.

turns.inner_thought: For the outlook, I really want the next-wave technical agenda: interoperability, scaling trade-offs, cross-chain design, privacy-preserving mechanisms. turns.inner_thought: I agree on strengthening the outlook, but for me it also needs to say something about standardization, regulatory stabilization, and institutional adoption over a medium horizon. That's what will make it feel relevant beyond computer science and position it as a broader field roadmap.
turns.utterance: I agree, and I think a strong outlook could also trace standardization, regulatory stabilization, and institutional adoption patterns. That would help the paper show not just what is changing technically, but how blockchain research is likely to consolidate over time.

turns.inner_thought: I need to make sure this doesn't turn into a giant protocol-heavy review. We can absolutely be systematic enough by anchoring the story in the most influential venues and landmark papers the lab already knows well, with some targeted checks around them. That keeps the workload realistic.
turns.utterance: My only caution is that I don't want this to become too heavy. I think we can still be systematic enough if we anchor it in the most influential venues and landmark papers and then build the framing carefully around those.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as we still define a clean protocol around the core indexed set. If I can specify search boundaries, inclusion logic, and a stable corpus, then the interpretive layer can sit on top of that and satisfy reviewers who care about defensibility.
turns.utterance: I think that's workable. We can keep it manageable by defining a clean review protocol around the core set and then layering the interpretive synthesis on top. That way the paper keeps a systematic backbone without reading like a methods exercise.

turns.inner_thought: We need a shortlist that is executable. The obvious three are technical evolution, applications across domains, and an outlook on emerging blockchain ecosystems. If we frame it well, we can draw on the literature the lab already has in hand and move quickly toward drafting.

turns.inner_thought: Great. I'll draft a concept note that makes the systematic backbone visible, maps applications broadly across domains, and closes with an outlook tied to future trajectories. If I do that carefully, we can later convert it into a stronger evidence synthesis and even a roadmap proposal.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'll sketch a concept note that preserves the systematic backbone, maps applications across domains, and ends with a strong outlook section tied to future trajectories. Then we can look at which framing gives us the best contribution story for the target journal.
